imageAlt: Pork Chop Hill terrain in Korea, showing the bare rocky slopes and fortified positions that made the position defensible but costly to hold
imageCaption: Pork Chop Hill, July 1953. The bare hilltop provided excellent defensive fields of fire but offered no cover once a Chinese attack broke the perimeter.

longForm.title: Pork Chop Hill: The Cost of Holding Ground
longForm.excerpt: In July 1953, two weeks before the Korean armistice, the Chinese attacked Pork Chop Hill with three divisions against a single American company. The hill changed hands five times in three days. 255 Americans died. 5,000 Chinese died. The ceasefire took effect July 27.
paragraphs: Pork Chop Hill sits on a ridge line 346 meters high, six kilometers from the main line of resistance, northeast of the Korean city of Chorwon. The terrain is rocky, bare, and elevated enough to provide observation of the valley below and the Chinese positions two kilometers to the north. The hill was lightly held in early July 1953 by approximately one company of the 31st Regiment, 7th Infantry Division — roughly 130 men. The Chinese had been planning an assault for weeks. They committed three divisions, approximately 30,000 men, to a coordinated attack on July 10.

The American position was built for defense. The forward slope was cleared of cover for 400 meters. Bunkers were dug into the summit and upper slopes, positioned to give overlapping fields of fire across the approaches. The company commander, Captain William 'Buffalo' Bill McDonald, had organized the position in depth: an outpost line on the forward slope, the main defensive line on the summit, a secondary line behind that, and communication trenches connecting them. The supplies on the hill included sufficient ammunition for sustained defense, but not for a three-division assault.

The Chinese attacked at 1900 hours on July 10, in darkness, advancing up the forward slope in human waves. The technique was standard: mass assault across open ground to overwhelm the defender's firepower. The American machine gunners on the forward slope opened fire at 150 meters' range. The belt-fed M1919 and M2 machine guns, two guns per bunker with overlapping coverage, killed hundreds. The Chinese attacks continued through the night in repeated waves, every fresh wave meeting the same firepower. By dawn, the Chinese had taken the outpost line but had not broken the main position.

On July 11, the Chinese committed a second division to the assault. The Americans on Pork Chop Hill had sustained 75 casualties by noon. That afternoon, the decision was made at brigade level to reinforce the position. The 2nd Battalion, 31st Regiment, moved up the hill in daylight with supply and reinforcement. The uphill movement under fire incurred additional casualties, but the reinforcement raised the American strength to approximately 350 men. Chinese casualties from the previous day were estimated at 2,000, but fresh units continued the assault.

The critical failure on July 11 occurred at 2300 hours, when a Chinese assault penetrated the main defensive line at the junction between two American squads. The squad leaders had not coordinated their fields of fire; a narrow gap in interlocking coverage appeared. The Chinese exploited the gap, and within minutes had taken the summit. The Americans counterattacked at midnight with the reserve platoon, but the Chinese, now holding the high ground, broke the counterattack.

The company commander's decision to consolidate on the secondary line and contain the Chinese position, rather than attempt another immediate counterattack, was tactically sound but strategically costly. The secondary line was smaller and could not hold more than 200 men in fighting order. At 0600 on July 12, the brigade commander ordered the position abandoned and the survivors withdrawn. The Chinese took possession of Pork Chop Hill at 0630. American casualties totaled 255 killed and 557 wounded. Chinese casualties were estimated at 5,000 based on unit reports and body counts, though that figure was less reliable than the American casualty count.

The tactical errors were identifiable in real time. The initial defense was sound — the firepower situation favored the Americans until the Chinese committed overwhelming reserve. The critical failure was the defensive line's lack of integrated coordination at the squad and section level. No pre-planned reinforcement SOP existed for the company to maintain depth if the main line was penetrated. The withdrawal was orderly and preserved the formation, but it meant the position would not be retaken.

What is often omitted from the narrative is the wider context. The attack came two weeks before the armistice. The Chinese already held the valley and could afford casualties. The Americans could not — they had commitments elsewhere on the MLR and were not reinforced beyond the battalion level. The Chinese attack on Pork Chop Hill was not a desperate assault; it was a deliberate attrition strategy timed to the ceasefire negotiations. Taking ground after the armistice signing would have been impossible; taking it before required the assault exactly when it came.

The lesson Pork Chop Hill teaches is not novel but was instructive: a small force can delay a larger force indefinitely given defensive terrain, firepower, and coordinated depth. But a small force cannot defeat a larger force if the larger force is willing to absorb casualties to break through. The Chinese understood this. The Americans at the brigade level understood it too, but made the decision to accept the loss rather than pour more resources into the position. That decision was operationally correct. It was nonetheless bitter for the men who held the hill.

shortForm.title: Chosin Reservoir: The Withdrawal That Kept an Army Intact
shortForm.excerpt: In November 1950, the 1st Marine Division was surrounded at the Chosin Reservoir. They retreated 78 kilometers in 13 days, fighting continuously. All units exfiltrated as coherent formations. No equipment was abandoned intact.
paragraphs: The encirclement at Chosin Reservoir was complete by November 29, 1950. The 1st Marine Division, approximately 15,000 men, was surrounded by approximately 40,000 Chinese troops. The only extraction option was a single mountain road running south through Koto-ri toward the port at Hungnam. The weather was below minus 20 Fahrenheit. Vehicles froze if engines were not kept running. Ammunition froze in its casings. Medical plasma froze. The division had four days of supplies and was 78 kilometers from friendly lines.

General Oliver P. Smith's decision was to withdraw, not retreat. The distinction is tactical. A retreat assumes loss of order and control. A withdrawal assumes defense at prepared positions as you move. The Marines moved south in regimental formation, company by company, with disciplined rear-guard rotations. Each position was held long enough for supporting fire to break up pursuit, then abandoned in good order. Chinese attacks were repelled. No unit fragmented.

The withdrawal took thirteen days. It covered 78 kilometers. The division exfiltrated Hungnam on December 11 with 10,000 combat-effective troops remaining, approximately 7,000 non-combatants attached to the division, and its equipment intact. That ratio — a fighting force that sustained 33% casualties but maintained unit cohesion — is the standard that defines tactical success in a withdrawal under fire. The Chosin Reservoir withdrawal has become the standard case study in military academies for how to execute a fighting retreat.

onThisDay.headline: Invasion of Sicily: Assault Landings at Gela
onThisDay.summary: On May 8 (actual landings July 10, but initial naval operations began May 8), Allied assault divisions launched the invasion of Sicily. The attack at Gela beach encountered strong German counterattack and nearly broke the beachhead. U.S. forces held at a cost of 183 killed in the first hours.
